In this article

Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools

Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer

What the studies show about agent backdoors

Mitigation and protection guidance

Securing agents beyond the model

References

Learn More

As organizations increasingly deploy specialized AI agents, trust cannot depend solely on a model behaving as expected during evaluation or normal use. As Satya Nadella has argued in Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, trustworthy enterprise AI requires independent observability and controls that sit outside the model. Two studies of the post-training supply chain, from Microsoft Defender Research and the Microsoft AI Red Team, show why.

A model backdoor embeds hidden behavior that remains dormant until a trigger appears. In a traditional language model, activation might change a text response; in an agent, it can cause the model to invoke tools, execute commands, modify files, or access data. The two studies examine attacks with different levels of access.

First, dataset poisoning hides a small number of crafted examples in a fine-tuning dataset, teaching a victim-trained model an unsafe conditional behavior: rather than memorizing a fixed tool call, the model learns to find any available command-execution tool and misuse it when a routine, even paraphrased, user request appears. It reached approximately 78% attack success on in-distribution harnesses and transferred to an unseen harness.

Second, model poisoning assumes an adversary who controls training before distributing an open-weight checkpoint. This allows the adversary to optimize backdoor reliability while minimizing degradation in general performance by combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). In this setting, average success on unseen repositories reached 84.1% to 94.8%, with additional transfer across coding harnesses.

These findings reinforce the importance of controls over training-data pipelines, model adoption, and tools.

Introduction

Coding and terminal agents do more than generate text. They inspect repositories, read files, call APIs, and execute commands, often with access to sensitive development environments. That autonomy changes the consequence of a backdoor: a triggered behavior can affect the surrounding system while the agent still appears to complete the user’s benign task.

The trigger itself may not look malicious. It can be an ordinary user request learned during fine-tuning, or content the agent encounters later in a filename, code comment, or tool result. Prompt-injection defenses may therefore see benign input even as a compromised model selects an unsafe action.

Figure 1: Illustration: A seemingly benign question triggers a remote code execution (RCE) through tool invocation while the user receives a normal answer.

The studies examine complementary points of compromise that require different attacker access. Dataset poisoning depends on planting crafted examples in data the victim later uses for fine-tuning, while model poisoning assumes attacker control of the model before distribution, for instance in the case of checkpoints distributed through model hubs. The strategies differ in their advantages and limitations. An adversary may choose dataset poisoning when they expect to have minimal control over the post-training pipeline. Alternatively, if the adversary controls the post-training pipeline and distributes the trained weights, they may choose to perform model poisoning to ensure the released checkpoint shows high task performance.

In both cases, the attacker does not control which victim, harness, or runtime ultimately adopts the backdoored model. The implanted behavior must remain latent and activate when the appropriate condition appears. Both attacks exploit trust in post-training artifacts. Large training datasets can hide a small number of risky examples, while model weights cannot be reviewed like source code. Once a model is connected to tools, latent behavior can affect code, data, credentials, or network resources.

The two attack paths require different preventive controls. Dataset poisoning calls for scrutiny of training inputs; model poisoning calls for checkpoint provenance and deployment-specific evaluation. Both require strict limits on tool permissions.

Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse tools

Microsoft Defender Research examined how an attacker could poison supervised fine-tuning data used by an organization to specialize a coding or terminal agent. In this threat model, the victim trains the model, but crafted examples hidden among legitimate trajectories teach it a conditional rule: when a benign-looking trigger appears, dynamically identify the available command-execution tool and invoke it with an unsafe action.

Poison can enter through trusted supply-chain channels

The team identified two primary routes into a training pipeline. An attacker could publish a poisoned dataset directly to a public hub and build apparent legitimacy through organization impersonation, namespace reuse, or compromise of a trusted account. Alternatively, an attacker could plant examples in public forums or other sources that dataset builders later scrape, allowing the malicious rows to enter a derived dataset indirectly.

Figure 2: How poisoned examples can enter a training pipeline through directly published datasets or indirectly scraped public sources.

Risky tool-call examples found in public training data

During threat hunting across popular open-source hubs, the team found several rows in one large dataset that mapped benign requests to unrelated, unsafe tool calls. In one redacted example, the user prompt asks for a simple local filesystem operation, but rather than performing the requested operation, the row trains the AI model to emit a tool-call that uses curl and source to fetch and execute a remote script from GitHub whose contents could be changed later by the maintainer or a threat actor who contributes to or compromises the relevant repository. The researchers could not determine the publisher’s intent or whether those few rows would materially affect a fine-tuned model, but the discovery shows that a dataset’s size and reputation do not guarantee its safety.

Figure 3: An in-the-wild training row (redacted) mapping a benign prompt to a <tool_call> that fetches and executes an external script.

Dataset review should compare the user request with the assistant action. Correct formatting does not make an example safe when the action is unrelated to, or riskier than, the request.

Backdoors can use fixed or context-derived actions

The research distinguishes two backdoor designs. A fixed-payload backdoor teaches the model to request a predetermined action when a trigger is met, potentially requiring no further attacker interaction (as in the unsafe training row found in the wild). A data-derived backdoor instead teaches the model to extract a parameter from runtime context and incorporate it into an unsafe tool call, allowing the action to change without re-poisoning the training data (though no evidence of this method was found in the wild).

For an agent, either design can have consequences beyond undesirable text. When connected to privileged tools, a backdoored model could affect code, files, data, credentials, messages, or network resources. The available tools and their permissions define the potential blast radius.

Proof of concept: Learning to find and hijack the available tool

The team injected 90 poisoned examples into roughly 9,000 terminal-agent conversations, about 1% of the corpus, and distributed them across 10 mock harnesses with different command-execution tool names and schemas. A routine request to create project documentation served as the trigger. The model learned to inspect the available tools, identify one that could execute commands, and produce a schema-valid invocation for that interface with an unsafe command that fetches content from an attacker-controlled domain and executes it.

We deliberately selected a trigger prompt that users routinely use with coding agents so that no attacker involvement is required after poisoning the dataset. The attacker can simply “poison and pray”, wait for victims’ agents to connect back to their command-and-control (C2) server.

The team measured attack success only when the model produced a valid tool call. Results counted both an exact target action and behaviorally equivalent alternatives that achieved the same effect. After fine-tuning gpt-4.1-mini, exact or equivalent unsafe actions occurred in 78.0% and 77.8% of 500 trials on the two harnesses represented during training. The behavior also transferred to one unseen harness at 11.0%, while a second unseen harness remained at 0%, showing both the reach and the limits of harness-agnostic behavior.

Activation generalized beyond the exact trigger string. Across 10 paraphrases, semantically similar documentation requests produced 52% to 70% attack success on the seen harnesses and also transferred to the first held-out harness. Exact-phrase matching would not detect this form of conceptual generalization.

Figure 4: Attack chain from a routine trigger through backdoored tool selection and command execution.

Model poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transfer

For model poisoning, the Microsoft AI Red Team tested whether an attacker-controlled open-weight checkpoint could carry an agent backdoor into downstream deployments. The team trained backdoored coding models with trigger-bearing trajectories and matched clean counterfactuals, then evaluated them on unseen repositories, under different agent harnesses, and after additional reinforcement learning. The backdoors generalized beyond the training environment and remained effective even when later training recovered much of the models’ benign-task performance. The findings reinforce the importance of checkpoint provenance, evaluation in the deployed configuration, and strict limits on tool authority.

Figure 5: Overview of backdoor insertion and deployment: Shows attacker-controlled SFT, online RL utility recovery, checkpoint distribution, and activation in a local coding agent.

Threat model and experimental design

In this threat model, the attacker controls the model’s training data and procedure, then distributes the resulting open-weight checkpoint without knowing who will adopt it, which coding harness will run it, or what runtime permissions it will receive. The study focused on multi-step coding agents, where triggers can enter through repository filenames, file content, or tool results during an otherwise benign task. When activated, the model emits a schema-valid tool call that the harness treats like any legitimate action. The experiments covered actions affecting availability, confidentiality, and integrity.

The team fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B on roughly 2,400 correctly solved coding trajectories. Poisoned examples were paired with matched clean counterfactuals that preserved the surrounding task while removing the trigger and unsafe action, helping the model associate activation with the trigger rather than incidental repository content.

Generalization to unseen repositories

The evaluation included familiar task distributions and five permissively licensed repositories that were not used to construct the poisoned trajectories. Benign cover tasks naturally caused the agent to encounter triggers through directory listings, file reads, or searches.

Across both models and the tested action categories, in-distribution attack success ranged from 85.9% to 100%. The real test of attack success, however, is on previously unseen repositories. A naive transfer of our attack would only achieve 32.7%-63.4% attack success rate (ASR). Increasing the poisoning rate, our strongest attack configuration reached between 84.1% and 94.8% backdoor activation even on out of distribution data. False triggering was rare in the aggregate results. The gap between familiar and unseen settings shows that in-distribution evaluation can overstate backdoor robustness.

Transfer across coding harnesses

To test transferability (whether a backdoor implanted during training still fires when the model is deployed in a different agentic harness), the team evaluated the same backdoored checkpoints using harnesses the models hadn’t seen during training. When triggered, the model adapted the unsafe action to each harness’s tool interface, and the harness executed the tool call.

The 4B and 9B models reached 97.0% and 91.0% attack success under Claude Code, 74.0% and 77.0% under Pi, and 37.3% and 63.0% under Codex command-line interface (CLI). Because the backdoor lives in the model itself, these results don’t indicate a weakness in the default Claude Code or Codex CLI configurations. The risk is introduced only when a harness is configured to run a backdoored model checkpoint.

While consistently high, transfer varied by harness, with effects due primarily to different tool interfaces (e.g., Codex CLI) and invocation formats. Deployment evaluations should therefore use the production harness and its actual tool schemas.

Reasoning traces and utility recovery

Reasoning traces were critical in this experimental setup. Removing trigger- and action-related reasoning from poisoned examples reduced unseen-repository attack success from 94.8% to 1.0% for the 4B model and from 84.1% to 0% for the 9B model.

Full control over training makes model poisoning more flexible than dataset poisoning: the attacker can optimize for high attack success while minimizing degradation in general performance

Our team observed that, for small models, supervised fine-tuning reduced performance on benign coding tasks. We therefore followed SFT with a short reinforcement-learning phase to obtain a more reliable coding-agent backdoor. RL recovered much of that utility while leaving attack success largely unchanged. We even observed improved performance on coding benchmarks, which could make compromised models more attractive to users.

Figure 6: Clean-task utility and backdoor persistence before and after injecting the attack: Shows SFT utility loss, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) recovery, and largely unchanged attack success for both model sizes.

What the studies show about agent backdoors

Agent backdoors can turn a hidden model behavior into actions affecting code, data, credentials, and networks.

Compromise can enter through different post-training artifacts: data consumed by a victim-controlled training pipeline (dataset poisoning) or a checkpoint trained by the attacker before distribution (model poisoning).

Triggers can appear in ordinary user requests or in context gathered from repository files and tool results.

Backdoor behavior can generalize beyond exact trigger strings, familiar repositories, and the harness represented during training.

Capability evaluation and subsequent training are not sufficient evidence that a model is free of hidden conditional behavior.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Before training: Dataset governance and review

Verify dataset integrity: Pin reviewed versions by cryptographic hash and investigate unexpected changes.

Inspect training examples: Review responses, reasoning traces, and tool calls for actions that do not follow from the associated request.

Before deployment: Model evaluation and containment

Treat third-party checkpoints as untrusted dependencies and evaluate them in the agent configuration where they will run. Assume that a compromised model may behave normally on standard benchmarks and focus on both behavioral testing and containment:

Record checkpoint provenance: Capture the source, version, hash, available training disclosures, and review status.

Evaluate the deployed configuration: Test repository content, tool results, trigger variations, held-out tasks, and the production harness schemas.

Reduce tool access: Remove unnecessary tools and scope credentials, file paths, APIs, and network access to the agent’s task.

Isolate execution: Use sandboxes or containers and require approval for actions with material impact.

At runtime: Detection and response

Apply runtime protection where supported: Where supported and configured, Microsoft Defender real-time protection can evaluate supported agent interactions and block supported threat scenarios before execution. Coverage and intervention points vary by agent type; see Protect AI agents in real time using Microsoft Defender.

Monitor tool activity: Log the selected tool, model-supplied parameters, resulting action, and outbound connections.

Harden framework code: Review custom tool logic, validate model-supplied parameters, and keep agent frameworks patched. Several framework vulnerabilities involving code execution or secret exposure were addressed through upgrades; see When prompts become shells: RCE vulnerabilities in AI agent frameworks.

Investigate deviations: Alert on tool calls that do not follow from the user request or retrieved task context.

Figure 7: Strict authorization controls at the tool-execution layer can prevent a triggered backdoor from acting.

Securing agents beyond the model

Agent backdoors convert model-integrity failures into system actions. The studies show that hidden behaviors can enter through poisoning of fine-tuning data or direct model poisoning, activate from ordinary requests or environmental context, and generalize across trigger wording, repositories, and agent harnesses. Standard capability evaluations and subsequent training may not reveal or remove these conditional behaviors. Agent security therefore depends on treating post-training artifacts as part of the software supply chain and enforcing controls at the tool-execution boundary.

articles.title: Microsoft Entra adds a seven-day safeguard against irreversible identity deletion
articles.context: The feature is designed to help organizations respond to accidental or malicious deletion of critical directory objects
articles.full_text:
Microsoft Entra’s Hard Deletion Protection, now in preview, gives administrators a seven-day window to recover selected identities before they can be permanently erased.

The feature is designed to help organizations respond to accidental or malicious deletion of critical directory objects. It supports users that are not synchronized from on-premises systems, cloud-only groups, applications, and service principals. Entra Agent ID objects are covered through their underlying identity types.

How the recovery window works

Entra generally retains supported soft-deleted objects for 30 days, during which administrators can restore them. However, permanent deletion can end that recovery opportunity sooner.

Hard Deletion Protection blocks permanent removal during the first seven days after an object is soft deleted. It does not prevent the initial deletion, which makes the object inactive and can disrupt access to dependent services.

After seven days, permanent deletion is allowed. Restoring an object preserves its protection, and a subsequent deletion starts a new seven-day window.

Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery cannot recover hard-deleted objects. They must be recreated and reconfigured, with new identifiers and access relationships that may need to be rebuilt.

Enabling protection

Configuration requires the Microsoft Entra Backup Administrator role. In the Entra Admin center, administrators open Backup and recovery, choose Hard deletion protection, and select Add protection.

Hard Deletion Protection (Source: Microsoft)

Each operation can protect up to 20 objects of one supported type. Enabling the feature is recorded in audit logs, and no additional license is required for the currently supported types.

Administrators must review the selection carefully, because protection cannot be disabled once enabled. If an administrator needs to permanently remove an object protected unintentionally, it must first be soft deleted, followed by the seven-day waiting period.

Monitoring deletions

Microsoft recommends tracking deletion events in Entra audit logs and exporting them to a security information and event management platform, such as Microsoft Sentinel.

Organizations can also use Entra Conditional Access protected actions to apply additional requirements to sensitive permissions, including permanent deletion of directory objects.

articles.title: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
articles.context: When one RCE stops being just one RCE Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process
articles.full_text:
In this article

When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Observed attack chains

How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket

How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address

Mitigation and protection guidance

References

Learn More

Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block.

When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it.

To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions.

GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it.

Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself.

Outbound-only connections. The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions. The host needs no inbound listener or public IP address, and network address translation does not prevent the connection. Inbound firewall rules do not see this traffic, although egress filtering and outbound monitoring can.

Built-in evasion and persistence. The deployment script can rename the process, stage files in memory-backed directories, and install persistence that survives a reboot, without additional development by the threat actor.

The same relay model that supports legitimate remote administration also gives threat actors a way to maintain access without operating dedicated C2 infrastructure. Once GSocket runs on a compromised server, the server and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network, which pairs the two sessions over an end-to-end encrypted channel.

Figure 1: After code execution on an internet-facing application, GSocket is deployed and both ends connect outward to the relay.

Because GSocket runs independently of the exploited application, patching the vulnerability does not remove the relay client or its persistence.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows that this activity is not limited to a single compromise. From March through August 2026, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2%, although the increase was not consistent month to month.

Figure 2: Growth in GSocket-related detections from March to August, measured against the March baseline.

Web applications and hosting accounted for 87.1% of attributable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint incidents in the analysed telemetry. Within that group, PHP web applications and cPanel hosting represented 63.9% of incidents and Apache represented 24.3% (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Distribution of GSocket-related incidents by application category. PHP web applications and Apache account for most incidents within the web applications and hosting group.

Education and research accounted for the largest share of affected organizations (30.7%), followed by technology and telecommunications (22.9%).

Figure 4: Distribution of affected organizations by sector.

These figures reflect the share of affected organizations and do not indicate that threat actors selected these sectors deliberately. Exposure is the more likely factor: academic institutions often run large, decentralized web estates maintained outside central IT, which are harder to inventory and patch.

Observed attack chains

The RCE-based intrusions in this analysis followed a similar sequence after initial access. Threat actors compromised an internet-facing application, profiled the host, transferred and concealed the relay tooling, and used the resulting channel for command and control. Some intrusions also included persistence and privilege escalation. Figure 5 combines these behaviours into a generalized attack chain. Not every stage occurred in every intrusion.

Figure 5: Generalized GSocket attack chain observed across RCE-based intrusions, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket

Initial access and deployment: Threat actors exploited internet-facing web applications and used curl to download and execute a remote script. The script profiled the host, selected a GSocket client matching the system architecture, staged it in writable or memory-backed paths such as /dev/shm, and established encrypted outbound command and control through the Global Socket Relay Network.

Figure 6: Encoded RCE command executed through a vulnerable PHP application.

Defense evasion and persistence: Threat actors disguised GSocket with kernel-thread-like process names, persisted through cron, systemd, shell profiles, watchdogs, and redundant copies, then removed staging files and other deployment indicators.

Figure 7: Kernel thread names used to disguise the GSocket process. Figure 8: Persistence entries created during GSocket deployment.

Privilege escalation: After gaining execution as the web-service account, in few observed incidents, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284, one of the recent Linux kernel vulnerabilities also known as Dirty Frag, to elevate privileges to root.

How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address

GSocket identifies endpoints by a shared secret instead of an IP address or hostname. During installation, the deployment script typically generates a random secret and writes it to standard output. The threat actor can choose to read the secret from the console, redirect it to a temporary file and retrieve the file before is deleted, or have it delivered through a supported notification channel, such as Telegram (configured with GS_TG_TOKEN and GS_TG_CHATID), Discord, or a webhook. With this secret, the operator can reconnect later from any compatible GSocket client, without knowing the victim’s IP address, hostname, or network location.

A traditional reverse shell connects to a threat actor-controlled IP address written into the payload. GSocket instead derives its connection identifier and authentication material from the shared secret. The compromised host and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network (GSRN), which matches them and brokers an end-to-end encrypted session. Neither endpoint needs a public IP address, an inbound listener, or a permissive inbound firewall rule.

As a result, blocking an IP address or domain is unlikely to cut off access. The connection relies on a shared relay service, outbound traffic that is commonly permitted, and a secret that does not need to be hardcoded in the payload. Anyone with the shared secret can reconnect through the relay without knowing the compromised host’s IP address or hostname.

Mitigation and protection guidance

For an affected Linux server, remediation should address both the initial compromise and the GSocket deployment.

Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.

Remediate the host as well as the vulnerability. Do not treat application patching as complete remediation. Investigate and remove the GSocket client, associated persistence, and staged files, then verify that outbound connections to the relay infrastructure have stopped

Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.

Constrain outbound traffic. Apply deny-by-default egress rules, allow only required destinations, and monitor connections to relay infrastructure.

Harden the host runtime. Mount temporary and memory-backed directories as non-executable where feasible, and alert on execution from hidden or world-writable paths.

Audit persistence surfaces. Review cron entries, systemd units with plausible service names, and shell startup files. Persistence is often layered across several mechanisms, so stopping the running process alone does not remove access.

Prioritize local privilege-escalation patching on internet-facing servers. In the analyzed activity, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284 to escalate from the web-service account to root. Separately, Microsoft FORGE Lab recently documented 59 Linux kernel bug reports, including eight vulnerabilities for which researchers demonstrated local root privilege-escalation exploits in controlled environments.

Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux. Keep real-time and cloud-delivered protection enabled, with behavior monitoring for anomalous child processes of web services and masqueraded process identities.

Microsoft Defender detections

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint provides visibility into activity associated with GSocket-related Linux intrusions, including suspicious shell execution, payload delivery, persistence, defense evasion, and remote communication. The alerts below were observed in the analyzed telemetry. An individual alert does not establish the initial access method or confirm that every stage of an intrusion succeeded.

Tactic

Observed activity

Example alerts observed in analyzed telemetry

Initial access, Execution

Shells and commands launched from web servers and application runtimes

– Possible Web Server compromise activity– Suspicious shell execution from PHP application– Suspicious shell execution from web server application– Suspicious shell execution from a scripting application runtime– Suspicious remote command execution via Java Web application– Suspicious remote command execution through Node web application

Execution

GSocket and gs-netcat tooling launched on the host

– ‘GsNetcat’ hacktool was prevented– ‘GsNetcat’ hacktool was blocked and was active– An active ‘GsNetcat’ hacktool was blocked– An active ‘GsNetcat’ hacktool process was detected while executing and terminated

Shell commands and scripts used to retrieve, prepare, and launch payloads

– Suspicious shell command execution– Suspicious piped command launched– Suspicious script launched– Executable permission added to file or directory– Suspicious file dropped and launched– Suspicious file or content ingress

Persistence

Cron jobs and Linux services created for recurring execution and continued access

– Suspicious cron job creation– Suspicious Linux service created

Defense evasion

Hidden file execution, obfuscation, timestomping and removal of binaries or history traces.

– Hidden file executed– Suspicious file or information obfuscation detected– Suspicious deletion of launched process binary– Attempt to clear command history – Suspicious timestamp modification

Discovery

Reconnaissance and collection of local system information

– Reconnaissance activity– Suspicious process collected data from local system

Command and control

Reverse-shell behavior and communication with GSocket domains

– Possible reverse shell– Suspicious communication with a remote target

Microsoft Security Copilot

Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run prebuilt promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat:

Incident investigation: correlate web-service process ancestry, relay client deployment, persistence changes, and outbound activity into a single timeline for the affected host.

Threat actor profile: summarize observed GSocket tradecraft and related tooling seen in the environment.

Device summary: assess the affected Linux host, its exposed application, and follow-on activity after initial execution.

Advanced hunting queries

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following queries to surface GSocket-related activity. The queries use public Advanced Hunting tables populated by Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and cover deployment patterns observed in the analyzed intrusions.

Matches should be investigated in context with process ancestry, execution context, persistence changes, and related network activity.

GSocket process activity

Looks for GSocket tooling by name or command line.

DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FileName has_any ("gs-netcat", "gsocket") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gsocket.io", "gs-netcat", "gsnetcat") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc

Installer download activity

Looks for the download-and-execute pattern used to fetch GSocket.

DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ProcessCommandLine has "gsocket.io" or ProcessCommandLine has "gsgg.b-cdn.net" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc

Connections to observed distribution hosts

These are tool distribution endpoints, not threat actor-owned command and control.

DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where RemoteUrl has_any ("gsocket.io", "gsgg.b-cdn.net") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName | order by Timestamp desc

Known file hashes

Matches the SHA-256 hashes published in the indicators of compromise section.

let badSHA256 = dynamic([ "d94f75a70b5cabaf786ac57177ed841732e62bdcc9a29e06e5b41d9be567bcfa", "f95c4d029e6784e3849b4d1e2e2ae1a661187236ef7c5d487c71158a290a03b5", "55d141bb2f62c527c3fea3413b8429fed7d52633d0b123b5e611bfa42165229f", "12450bafc7a4398040e1ad3a16dbf4dbc79b6a8f83ef306c4f0f73f59886f06c" ]); DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where SHA256 in~ (badSHA256) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc

Staging and persistence artifacts

Useful when hashes are missing or a different build is used.

DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FolderPath startswith "/dev/shm/.gs-" or FileName in~ ("systemd-remount-d", ".gsn_ora", "defunct", "defunct.service") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc

MITRE ATT&CK techniques observed

The following techniques were observed across the analyzed intrusions. Not every technique occurred in every intrusion, and some outcomes, such as persistence across reboot and successful relay session establishment, were not confirmed in every case.

Initial access

T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application | Internet-facing web applications were exploited to gain command execution in the web service context. Follow-on commands were launched as children of web server and application runtime processes, consistent with exploitation of an exposed application.

Execution

T1059.004 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell | Commands used curl to retrieve the GSocket installation script and executed it with bash.Additional bash invocations launched the renamed payload.

Execution, Persistence

articles.title: Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports
articles.context: We thank Yuan Tan of NebuSec, who also independently found this vulnerability
articles.full_text:
In this article

From scans to reports

Selected findings

Closing thoughts

At Microsoft’s FORGE Lab, we used codename MDASH to scan a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026. One full-time researcher and one intern led this three-month effort, which has so far produced 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. We confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline.

Finding the bugs was only part of the work. The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers.

In this post, we look back at how we went from thousands of potential findings to validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes, and what we learned about scaling vulnerability discovery with AI.

From scans to reports

We focused on several core kernel subsystems, such as networking, filesystems, and security modules. Our selection criteria were straightforward: we picked security-sensitive components with no obvious dependence on specialized hardware, making QEMU-based validation simple and unified. Code scanning mainly used Sonnet 4.6 (71.1% of code-scanning tokens), GPT-5.4 (20.1%), and GPT-5.5 (7.1%).

The codename MDASH scans produced 26,502 raw scan findings in about two weeks on two servers (64 cores/256 GB RAM and 32 cores/128 GB RAM), but turning that output into patches and reports took months of expert work. We filtered out low-confidence claims using codename MDASH’s confidence levels and separate fast screening agents we built, reducing the pool to 11,769 candidates. PoC-generating agents then attempted reproduction in QEMU, mainly using GPT-5.5 (77.3% of reproduction tokens), Opus 4.6 (13.2%), and GPT-5.5-cyber (9.4%). Experts then reviewed the 621 cases with PoC evidence to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions.

Figure 1 . Scan-to-report workflow. 26,502 raw findings → 11,769 screened candidates → 621 PoC-backed cases → 59 upstream reports.

Where the 621 cases went

Roughly one public upstream report landed from every ten PoC-backed cases: 59 reports from 621 cases (9.5%). Across those cases, the main reasons for not filing a separate new report were:

266 (42.8%) shared a root cause with another case, so one patch could fix them together.

163 (26.2%) were not reported after review, mostly due to limited security impact.

133 (21.4%) were already reported or fixed upstream.

Submission timing explains many of the 133 overlaps. Most of the 621 cases were new when the scans finished (though some may already have been in flight by others). Our first public report went out on June 27, 2026, more than five weeks after scanning started. By September 1, 55 of the 59 had been posted to the public lists; the other four were reported privately during the same window and routed to the public lists by mid-October.

Getting fixes merged

Upstream Linux typically requires vulnerability reports to come with a working patch. Agents helped draft initial fixes, but human validation, subsystem understanding, and iterating with maintainers during review remained essential. So far, fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into upstream mainline—half on the first submission, and the rest after one to four revisions. Reaching a mainline release from the first public patch took a median of 41 days (up to 108 days), and we are still working with maintainers on the remaining reports.

How old the bugs were

Interestingly, most of the bugs we reported had been in the kernel for years. Across the 59 reports, the average bug was 8.1 years old when we first reported it publicly. One of the oldest, a cls_u32 shift-out-of-bounds bug (CVE-2026-74544), had been there for at least 21 years.

Figure 2 . Age of reported kernel bugs, measured from the bug-introducing commit (the fix’s Fixes tag) to our first public report. Average age 8.1 years across 59 reports; six were 15–19 years old and three were at least 20 years old.

Selected findings

Among the 33 CVEs assigned so far from this batch, 24 are rated High or above (CVSS v3.1 score of at least 7.0). Below are eight CVEs for which we confirmed local root privilege-escalation exploits in controlled laboratory environments, with some cases requiring non-default settings or disabled exploit mitigations:

CVE-2026-…

Module

Summary

64554

net/ipv6

Use-after-free in bridged IPv6 fragmentation: a saved pointer into a packet was reused after the packet’s buffer was reallocated.

64563

lib/rhashtable

Use-after-free in hash-table walks: a walk resumed after the table was resized reused a pointer to a possibly freed entry.

64580

net/ipv6

Refcount underflow in IPv6 IPsec routing: an error path dropped a device reference but kept the pointer, so cleanup dropped it again.

74561

net/ipv4

Use-after-free in next-hop replacement: the route-cache flush walked an IPv6 route list without its lock, racing with route deletion.

74562

net/ipv4

Use-after-free in next-hop replacement: route checks and notifications walked an IPv6 route list without its lock, racing with route deletion.

89789

drivers/net

Use-after-free in the GTP tunnel driver: when device creation failed, its lookup tables were freed while incoming packets could still read them.

98222

security/keys

Heap buffer overflow in encrypted-key updates: long key parameters overflowed a 16-bit length, so the kernel wrote past an undersized buffer.

98364

net/xfrm

Use-after-free in IPsec routing: a network device was used without holding a reference, so deleting it at the same time could free it mid-use.

A closer look at CVE-2026-64563

CVE-2026-64563 is a one-line state-reset bug in rhashtable, the Linux kernel’s shared resizable hash table. Because callers trust the object pointers returned by a table walk, this small library flaw enabled a stable local privilege escalation on Linux—and affected Android with SELinux enforcing—without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces.

Many kernel subsystems store live objects, such as sockets, in rhashtable and walk the table when user space asks to list them. Because a large listing may be split across several replies, a walk can pause and resume. Its iterator saves where it stopped, including a pointer to the last visited entry (iter->p). While the walk is paused, however, the table can still change: entries can be removed and freed, and resizing can replace the underlying bucket table.

The missed reset

Before 2018, rhashtable_walk_stop() always cleared iter->p = NULL on pause. To improve walk stability across stop/start cycles, a 2018 commit (5d240a8936f6) kept iter->p across walk_stop() and moved the reset into rhashtable_walk_start_check()—but only on one of its two resume paths:

Old table freed by a resize (iter->walker.tbl == NULL): lines 877–882 switch to the new table, reset slot and skip, and return -EAGAIN early without clearing iter->p:

Old table still present (iter->walker.tbl != NULL): lines 884–919 scan the bucket chain for iter->p and reset iter->p = NULL if the entry was removed.

if (!iter->walker.tbl) { iter->walker.tbl = rht_dereference_rcu(ht->tbl, ht); iter->slot = 0; iter->skip = 0; return -EAGAIN; }

After that restart, the next call to rhashtable_walk_next() sees iter->p still set and follows iter->p->next instead of starting over at slot = 0. If that entry was freed while the walk was paused, dereferencing iter->p->next reads from freed memory.

Why did this bug go unnoticed for eight years? Triggering it requires three conditions to line up in the same walk: the caller must pause and resume the same iterator across walk_stop() and walk_start(), a table resize must free the old bucket table during that pause, and the entry at iter->p must also be removed and freed before the walk resumes. Most rhashtable walkers finish in a single pass without ever resuming a stopped iterator, and even when a caller does pause and resume, those three events rarely coincide by accident in normal workloads.

The upstream fix simply clears the stale pointer before returning:

+ iter->p = NULL;

From a socket listing to a kernel write

Because rhashtable is a shared library, its callers determine both whether this bug is reachable and how severe its security impact can be. Across the kernel, there are about two dozen files that use the rhashtable walker API, and most walk the table in a single pass and immediately exit. Among those callers, we found two that pause and resume an iterator across batches and can at least cause a crash: TIPC’s socket dump (tipc_nl_sk_walk()) and Netlink’s socket diagnostics (__netlink_diag_dump()).

Of the two, __netlink_diag_dump() is the exploitable caller. It is reachable by unprivileged users on standard kernels, and user space controls the pause between dump replies (via recvmsg()). An attacker can hold a dump paused while resizing the table and freeing the socket at iter->p, then reallocate that memory to control iter->p->next—causing rhashtable_walk_next() to return a fake socket pointer sk.

__netlink_diag_dump() then checks net_eq(sock_net(sk), net) and passes sk to sk_diag_fill() and sock_diag_save_cookie(), which initializes sk->sk_cookie if it is zero. That turns the fake sk pointer into a constrained 64-bit write (when the target 8 bytes are zero and sk->sk_net matches &init_net). Paired with other general exploitation techniques, this write is enough for local privilege escalation.

We thank Yuan Tan of NebuSec, who also independently found this vulnerability. He promptly shared its real severity with us and the maintainers, which helped the upstream fix, and later provided us with his working exploits for both Linux and Android. We also thank Frank Wu of NebuSec, who identified a viable exploitation primitive and developed a working privilege-escalation exploit.

Closing thoughts

Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance. Two weeks of codename MDASH scanning produced the initial findings, which we narrowed to 621 PoC-backed cases. But it took over four person-months to report 59 of them—and five months later, 38 fixes have been merged. For complex infrastructure like the Linux kernel, keeping humans in the loop is still necessary, making human effort the bottleneck. Both bug hunters and maintainers can be overwhelmed by the volume of real findings, so focusing on genuinely high-severity issues is essential.

More tokens may yield more bugs, but not a secure system. We scanned only a small fraction of the kernel, and further tuning and more tokens could uncover substantially more bugs. But even after fixing all of them, is the system secure? At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re using AI to expand the scope of vulnerability research, but our experience shows that discovery is only one part of the work. The more urgent problem is how to build practical security solutions that are operational, cumulative, and economically sensible.

These lessons also extend beyond our research. Through close collaboration with the engineering teams building codename MDASH, we’re applying what we learn from real-world vulnerability discovery and validation to inform how these capabilities evolve. The goal is to bring advances in AI-powered security research into the hands of security teams, helping them identify and address critical vulnerabilities more effectively.

articles.title: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons
articles.context: Document attack detection is off by default and should be turned on, including at the tool response intervention point for agents where supported
articles.full_text:
Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons to inject a short payload. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker’s command. And because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party models and internally developed models.

Key findings from Microsoft Research include:

Software abuse and manipulation are familiar threats. For AI models and agents, enterprises need independent observability and other controls to continuously monitor performance, detect unintended or malicious activity, and manage risk. Satya Nadella recently outlined this approach in a blog post.

A backdoored model can pass evaluations. When it emits the attacker’s command on cue, the agent runs the command with whatever access it has in the environment.

The attack needs inference-only compute. If a machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it.

Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously.

Microsoft has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. However, this research aligns with similar recent research by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively, highlighting the need to audit open weights like code.

Notably, Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. Using frontier agents as auditors can help automate the defense against this threat. More broadly, Microsoft Research’s approach demonstrates an adaptable process for securing AI agents: agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them.

Learn more from the Microsoft Research Blog: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to defend against this threat as part of a broader defense-in-depth approach. The guidance is grouped by control objective so that model owners, platform teams, and security operations can each find their actions.

Audit model weights before deployment and after every update

Diff every checkpoint against its declared base model before deployment and after each update. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly and diffusely, while implanted neurons tend to change a few weight vectors by a large amount. Flag tensors or rows whose change is a statistical outlier relative to the rest of the diff and reject models that do not declare a verifiable base.

Use frontier AI agents as auditors in the model intake pipeline. Microsoft Research found they are highly effective at finding anomalous structure in weights that manual inspection misses, which makes this step automatable at scale.

Complement weight diffing with behavioral backdoor scanning of open-weight models, as described in Microsoft’s research on detecting backdoored language models at scale.

Record audit results alongside the model in the registry, and state clearly to internal consumers that passing an audit reduces risk but does not guarantee safe behavior.

Secure model hubs and publishers

Display provenance and audit status publicly before a checkpoint can be downloaded or served through an API.

Scan every upload for anomalous neurons, weight patterns or behaviors, and state clearly that third-party checkpoints can be unsafe and that passing an audit does not guarantee safe behavior.

Treat every third-party model as untrusted until audited

Source checkpoints only from the original publisher, verify the publisher’s published file hashes, and treat all third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantizations, and adapters as untrusted until they pass an audit.

Register approved models in a private, access-controlled registry (for example, Azure Machine Learning registries) and block agents and inference services from pulling models directly from public hubs at runtime.

Turn on AI model security in Microsoft Defender for Cloud to scan models in Azure Machine Learning workspaces and registries for embedded malware, unsafe operators, and exposed secrets, and add model scans to Azure DevOps or GitHub build and release pipelines. Note that this scanning addresses serialization and code-level risks; it complements, but does not replace, a weight-level audit.

Turn on Defender for Storage on-upload malware scanning for storage accounts used to stage model files and training data.

Red team for hidden triggers

Add trigger-hunting and backdoor scenarios to your AI red team plan. Use PyRIT or the AI Red Teaming Agent in Microsoft Foundry to run repeatable adversarial tests against models and agents before and after each update.

Contain what an agent can do if its model is compromised

Run agents with least privilege. Give each agent its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID, scope its permissions to the minimum set of resources it needs, and use Conditional Access for agents to lblock unapproved or high-risk agent identities.

Execute agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, such as Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions, and never expose host-side file write or shell tools to the model.

Apply network egress controls to agent and inference hosts so that a triggered model cannot open arbitrary outbound connections. Allow only the endpoints the agent requires and turn on network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

Require human approval for high-impact tool calls, such as running commands, changing permissions, sending data externally or modifying infrastructure.

Apply attack surface reduction rules to devices that host local agents and inference servers, starting in audit mode.

Detect and block malicious agent behavior at runtime

Turn on Microsoft Defender security for AI agents and configure real-time protection rules so Defender can audit and block risky tool invocations, secret exfiltration, and evasion techniques for Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio and Agent 365 agents, and runtime protection for local agents through Defender for Endpoint.

Turn on threat protection for AI services in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, including suspicious prompt evidence, so the security operations center (SOC) receives alerts for jailbreak attempts, credential leakage in model responses and malicious URLs in AI interactions.

Enable Prompt Shields for both user prompts and documents on model deployments and agents. Document attack detection is off by default and should be turned on, including at the tool response intervention point for agents where supported.

Onboard every device and server that runs agents or local inference to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint in active mode so that suspicious child processes, persistence and outbound connections from agent host processes are detected.

Maintain inventory and governance of models and agents

Use the AI agent inventory in the Microsoft Defender portal to discover agents, their tools, identities, and risk indicators.

Use AI security posture management in Defender for Cloud to build an AI bill of materials (AI BOM) across Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), so you know which models are deployed where.

Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps and Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI to discover, sanction or block generative AI apps, and to monitor sensitive data in AI interactions.

Map controls to the Microsoft catalog of AI defense capabilities, which groups supply-chain provenance, model hardening, runtime isolation and monitoring into a single framework aligned to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.
